title: Fact-Checking Cancer Information on Social Media in Japan: Retrospective Study Using Twitter
screen_reason: Two oncologists independently fact-checked the medical claims in the 100 most-liked eligible Japanese-language cancer tweets (posted Aug-Sep 2022) on a 1-5 accuracy scale, with a rounded mean of 3 or more defined as misinformation: 44/100 (44%) contained misinformation (Cohen kappa 0.50). That is an explicit falsity share of items with a stated denominator (CONTENT). A parallel 1-5 harm rating gives 31/100 (31%) harmful, recorded separately as OTHER because harm is not veracity (1% of tweets were factual AND harmful).

estimates.date: Tweets posted August 2022 to September 2022; API query run 29 September 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 most-liked eligible Japanese-language cancer tweets judged to contain misinformation by two independent oncologist reviewers
estimates.value_raw: 44% of the leading 100 tweets contained misinformation (n=44; kappa=0.50, 95% CI 0.38-0.65)
estimates.denominator: the 100 most-liked tweets among 276 eligible cancer-information tweets, themselves drawn from 69,857 Japanese tweets mentioning 'cancer' (19,325 retweets excluded, leaving 50,532; narrowed to the 2,000 most-liked; 1,360 cancer-related; 276 meeting the content criteria)
estimates.definition: each reviewer scored the tweet's medical claims 1 = true, 2 = mostly true, 3 = both true and false, 4 = mostly false, 5 = false; the two physicians' average was rounded to the nearest whole number and a score of 3 or more counted as misinformation (reasons: Unproven, Disproven, Inappropriate application, Strength of evidence mischaracterized, Misleading, Other; multiple reasons allowed)
estimates.misinfo_def: "In the analysis of accuracy, the reviewers scored each tweet from 1 to 5 points (1: true, 2: mostly true, 3: both true and false, 4: mostly false, and 5: false). The average of the 2 physicians was rounded to the nearest whole number, with scores of 3 or more indicating misinformation and scores of 2 or less indicating factual information."
estimates.source_quote: Following expert review, 44% of the leading 100 tweets contained misinformation (n=44; κ=0.50, 95% CI 0.38-0.65; Figure 2 A)
estimates.page_loc: Results, first paragraph; Figure 2A; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent reviewers, both physicians specialising in oncology practising at a cancer centre or university hospital in Japan, using a 4-question assessment adapted from Johnson et al's accuracy/credibility instrument; scores averaged and rounded; Cohen kappa = 0.50 (95% CI 0.38-0.65) for the misinformation rating - only moderate agreement. No external fact-check organisation or guideline document was used as the standard.
estimates.moderator_quote: Tweet data were retrospectively collected from August 2022 to September 2022 by querying the Twitter app programming interface with the keyword "cancer" in Japanese ... On the review process, we first narrowed down all the acquired tweets to the 2000 tweets with the most "likes" ... The 100 tweets with the most "likes" were finally extracted from the eligible tweets.
estimates.notes: denom_selection=curated because the denominator is a likes-truncated top-100 slice (twice truncated: top 2,000 then top 100), so the estimate describes the most-liked cancer content, not cancer tweets in general - an important upward-bias caveat for pooling. breadth=misleading: the numerator spans Unproven, Inappropriate application, Strength-of-evidence mischaracterised and Misleading as well as Disproven, so it is broader than outright falsehood. Reviewer agreement is only moderate (kappa 0.50). Internal inconsistencies in the paper, all in the reason breakdown rather than the headline value: the abstract gives Unproven as 29/94 (40.4%) while Table 1 gives 38 (40.4%) - 40.4% of 94 is 38, so the abstract's 29 appears to be a typo; the abstract gives Misleading as 18/94 (18%) and Table 1 as 18 (19.1%); and the tweet total is 69,875 in the abstract but 69,857 in the Results. The 44/100 value itself is stated identically in the abstract, Results and Figure 2A.

estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 most-liked eligible Japanese-language cancer tweets judged to contain harmful information by two independent oncologist reviewers
estimates.value_raw: In total, 31% of tweets were classified as containing harmful information (n=31; kappa=0.62, 95% CI 0.44-0.79)
estimates.denominator: the same 100 most-liked eligible cancer tweets
estimates.definition: harmful information was any tweet rated 'Probably harmful' or 'Definitely harmful' by at least one of the two reviewers on a 1-5 harm scale (reasons: Harmful action, Harmful inaction, Harmful interactions, Economic harm, Other)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Harmful information was defined as any rating by at least one reviewer of 'Probably harmful' or 'Definitely harmful'; the remaining options were classified as Safe information."
estimates.source_quote: In total, 31% of tweets were classified as containing harmful information (n=31; κ=0.62, 95% CI 0.44-0.79; Figure 2 B)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two oncologist reviewers; harm rated 1-5 with an any-reviewer threshold (deliberately lenient, unlike the averaged accuracy rule); Cohen kappa = 0.62.
estimates.moderator_quote: In harm analysis, the reviewers gave each tweet a score from 1 to 5 (1: Definitely not harmful, 2: Probably not harmful, 3: Uncertain, 4: Probably harmful, and 5: Definitely harmful).
estimates.notes: Coded OTHER (not CONTENT) and borderline=true: harmfulness is not a veracity judgement - the paper itself reports 1% of tweets as Factual-Harmful, so a wholly accurate tweet can carry the label. Should be excluded from any prevalence pool; kept because it is one of the paper's two headline numbers and because 30% of tweets were BOTH misinformation and harmful, which an adjudicator may need in order to see that the 44% and 31% overlap heavily rather than being additive. Note the harm threshold is 'at least one reviewer', a looser rule than the averaged accuracy threshold.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The 2x2 cross-tabulation was not written as rows because its cells are subsets of the two rows above: Factual-Safe 55% (55/100), Factual-Harmful 1% (1/100), Misinformation-Safe 14% (14/100), Misinformation-Harmful 30% (30/100); 68.9% (30/44) of misinformation tweets also contained harmful information. The Misinformation-Harmful cell (30%) is the closest thing to a strict 'harmful misinformation' prevalence if the review wants one. (2) Reason categories are multiple-response counts over reason-selections, not tweets (denominator 94 selections for misinformation, 59 for harm), so they are not shares of tweets and cannot be used as prevalence: Unproven 38 (40.4%) [abstract says 29], Disproven 19 (20.2%), Inappropriate application 4 (4.3%), Strength of evidence mischaracterized 14 (14.9%), Misleading 18 (19.1%) [abstract 18%], Other 1 (1.1%); Harmful action 9 (15.2%), Harmful inaction 43 (72.9%), Harmful interactions 3 (5.1%), Economic harm 3 (5.1%), Other 1 (1.7%). (3) Engagement comparisons are medians, not shares, so no rows: likes - factual median 93 vs misinformation 92.5 (P=.24), harmful 95 vs safe 75.0 (P=.04); retweets - misinformation median 29.0 vs factual 7.5 (P=.01), harmful 35.0 vs safe 8.0 (P=.002); overall medians 76.5 likes and 13.5 retweets. There is NO share of retweets carrying misinformation, so no SHARING row can be built. (4) No exposure/reach/recall measure is reported; the study never reports what share of all 69,857 (or 50,532) cancer tweets was misinformation, only the top-100 slice.

rob.design: Retrospective cross-sectional content analysis. Twitter API query (run 29 Sep 2022, Jupyter Notebook) for Japanese-language tweets containing 'cancer' posted Aug-Sep 2022: 69,857 tweets, 19,325 retweets excluded (50,532 left), narrowed to the 2,000 most-liked, then 1,360 cancer-related, then 276 meeting content criteria, then the 100 most-liked analysed. Two independent oncologist reviewers scored accuracy (1-5, averaged and rounded, >=3 = misinformation; kappa 0.50, 95% CI 0.38-0.65) and harm (1-5, any-reviewer 'probably/definitely harmful'; kappa 0.62, 95% CI 0.44-0.79), following Johnson et al's method, with structured reasons and multiple selections allowed. Mann-Whitney U tests for likes/retweets; Prism 9. Authors' stated limitations: retrospective design and selection bias (mitigated by excluding Breast Cancer Awareness Month / Pink Ribbon Week and a cancer-eradication campaign), short 2-month window, small number of included tweets, high variability in likes and retweets with outliers excluded, and the subjectivity of accuracy and harm judgements. Additional weaknesses for this review: the denominator is a doubly likes-truncated top-100 sample so the estimate is not representative of cancer tweets generally; the ground truth is expert opinion with only moderate agreement; and 'cancer' as a single keyword may miss disease-specific misinformation.
